item.title: Exposing biased risk estimation of emergency service disruptions during urban floods
item.description:
Xiyu Pan, Neda Mohammadi, John E. Taylor
npj Urban Sustainability
DOI: 10.1038/s42949-026-00473-3
Abstract Urban flooding severely disrupts emergency services. Equitable mitigation requires identifying if socially vulnerable neighborhoods face disproportionate travel delays. Previous research overlooks estimation biases, where underestimating risks for vulnerable populations can skew assessments, ultimately hindering effective efforts to reduce risk inequities. Comparing modeled and observed ambulance response times during the 2016 Hurricane Matthew flood in Virginia Beach, we found travel time for low-income communities was underestimated by an average of 5.7 min compared with an underestimation of 1.9 min for high-income communities, which captures only 35.8% of actual risk inequity. This bias was found to be associated with greater traffic congestion and more ambulance stations being closed or running out of capacity in lower-income communities, neither of which is considered in existing approaches. This discrepancy in modeled response time underscores an improved estimation of emergency service flood disruptions to enhance healthcare safety and promote equitable risk mitigation.
